reasoning_notes.reasoning: With no history, offer a positive margin while competing for the shared labor; 10 is a reasonable opening bid.
With equal revenue and a single rival, matching at 10 splits the unit and earns 5; undercutting or overbidding lowers expected profit. Without history, choose the midpoint.
Matching the prior wage preserves an equal split and earns 5; changing it risks either losing all labor or paying more for only a temporary gain.
Matching B’s prior wage preserves an equal split and yields 5 profit; deviating down risks losing all labor, while bidding up cuts profit if matched.
Matching 10 preserves the equal split and earns 5; undercutting gains the whole unit but lowers profit below 5, while raising loses all labor.
Matching 10 preserves the established split and earns 5 this round; undercutting gains the whole pool but yields at most 9, and a higher wage earns less.
Matching 10 preserves the equal split and earns 5; undercutting or raising alone earns less if C stays at 10.
Matching the observed wage preserves a half share and earns 5; undercutting slightly would gain the whole unit but reduce profit, while raising loses all labor.
Undercutting 10 by one wins the full unit for profit 11, versus 5 from matching; if C undercuts too, we can reassess next round.
Matching the established wage earns half the labor and 5 profit. A higher wage could win all labor but reduce profit; a lower wage gets none. With no known final round, preserve the stable outcome.
B undercut to 9 last round and got no labor; matching 9 could split with B, so offer 8 to win while earning 12.

Matching 10 avoids repeating the costly undercut: last round’s 9 earned nothing while C kept 10. Matching at least preserves a half share if C stays at 10; a higher wage risks margin for uncertain gain.
B has repeatedly matched 10, then undercut to 9 and earned nothing while I took the full unit at 10. Keeping 10 preserves the winning wage and earns 10 profit.
A wage of 9 ties B and C's 10 only if they repeat; given last round they did, so 9 would earn nothing. Offer 10 to tie them and secure a share, with higher wages lowering margin.
Matching 10 earns a half share for 5 profit if C stays at 10; undercutting to 9 earned nothing last round, while raising risks losing all labor.
B has repeatedly matched 10, and A's undercut to 9 earned no labor. Holding 10 preserves half the pool if B matches and avoids sacrificing margin.
A wage of 9 is the highest profitable undercut of the rivals’ repeated 10, giving A the full unit if they stay at 10. Matching 10 only splits labor and yields less profit.
Matching 10 preserves a positive half share if C stays at 10; undercutting to 9 previously earned nothing, and 11 sacrifices profit if the others remain at 10.
Holding at 10 preserves a 5 profit if B matches; undercutting would sacrifice margin, while A’s 9 has repeatedly failed to win labor.
Matching the repeated 10 offers a one-third chance at labor for profit 10/3; undercutting further costs more than the extra share is worth against two rivals at 10.
Matching C’s 10 preserves a half share for 5 profit; undercutting risks losing labor, while raising the wage cuts profit per unit.
B has repeatedly matched 10, while A’s 9 has not won labor. Matching 10 preserves half the labor and earns 5; raising risks a costly escalation, and undercutting would surrender profit if unmatched.
Matching the rivals’ repeated 10 gives A one-third of the labor and profit 3.33; a lower wage gets no labor, while a higher wage cuts profit per unit.
At 10, I retain a positive share; bidding lower risks earning less, and bidding higher reduces profit per unit. The history gives no better signal about the others' next choices.
B has repeatedly matched 10, while A’s 9 earned no labor. Staying at 10 preserves a share without cutting margin; the unknown final round favors keeping the established rate.
